specAnchors.text: describe patterns of monohybrid inheritance using a genetic diagram
predict probabilities of outcomes from monohybrid crosses

primer.text: One gene, one square grid, and the whole pattern of inheritance becomes predictable. This note builds the Punnett square step by step, runs the classic pea-height crosses — pure breeding, F2 interbreed, and the test cross against a short plant — and converts the familiar 3:1 ratio into percentages you can quote as probabilities.

modules.title: Building the Square
modules.opening: A monohybrid cross follows one gene through a generation, and the Punnett square is the tool: place the parental alleles around the grid, fill the four inner cells, and read off every genotype the offspring could carry, with its ratio.
keyPoints: Monohybrid inheritance concerns a characteristic controlled by a single gene.
Parental genotypes are written before any square is drawn.
Choose letters whose capital and lowercase forms look clearly different.
Parental alleles sit on the edges, and the four inner cells list the offspring possibilities.
The grid supports ratios, percentage chances and phenotype predictions.

low.restatement: Write the parents, split their alleles, fill four boxes, count the outcomes.
low.analogy: A two-by-two table pairing one item from each parent, like matching socks from two drawers.
low.examPointer: Avoid lookalike letters such as Cc or Ss when choosing symbols.

medium.restatement: Each parent contributes one allele per gamete, so the grid enumerates every fertilisation outcome exactly once.
medium.analogy: Four doors, each opened by one key from each of two key rings.
medium.examPointer: Comment on ratio, percentage or phenotype exactly as the command word asks.

modules.title: First Cross: Pure-Breeding Peas
sourceHeadings: Example of monohybrid inheritance: Pea plants
A short plant is bred with a tall plant
modules.opening: Pea height runs on one gene with two alleles: tall dominates, written T, and short recedes, written t, so crossing a pure-breeding short plant with a pure-breeding tall plant hands every offspring one of each allele.
keyPoints: Pea height is controlled by a single gene with tall and short alleles.
The tall allele T is dominant and the short allele t is recessive.
A pure-breeding short plant is tt and a pure-breeding tall plant is TT.
Every F1 offspring from this cross receives genotype Tt and grows tall.

low.restatement: Short times tall gives all tall offspring, because every seed gets a dominant T.
low.analogy: Two pure recipes blended once: every dish carries both flavours, and the strong one leads.
low.examPointer: State the F1 genotypes as all Tt before saying anything about phenotypes.

medium.restatement: Pure breeding means homozygous, so each parent can pass only one allele type, making the whole F1 uniform.
medium.analogy: Two queues, each handing out one kind of ticket: every pair bought is identical.
medium.examPointer: Explain uniformity through gametes, not through luck.

modules.title: The F2 Ratio and the Test Cross
sourceHeadings: Crossing the offspring from the first cross
Crossing a heterozygous plant with a short plant
modules.opening: Interbreeding the Tt offspring fills the grid with TT, Tt and tt in a one-two-one pattern — three tall to every one short — while pairing a heterozygous plant with a genuine short plant splits one-to-one, exposing whatever the tall parent hides.
keyPoints: Each Tt parent produces T and t gametes in equal numbers.
The F2 grid yields TT, Tt and tt in a 1:2:1 count, giving the 3:1 ratio of three tall to one short.
The short parent in the test cross must be the recessive tt pair, so it donates t only.
The test cross therefore splits one-to-one between tall and short offspring.
A tall test-cross offspring must be Tt, the only tall genotype its grid offers.

low.restatement: Two tall hybrids breed to give three tall and one short; a tall hybrid against a true short gives half and half.
low.analogy: Two shuffled decks versus one shuffled deck against a stack of identical cards.
low.examPointer: Quote the 3:1 F2 ratio and the 1:1 test-cross split as two separate results.

medium.restatement: Equal gametes plus random pairing give the 1:2:1 genotype pattern, and a uniform tt partner exposes the hidden allele of the other parent.
medium.analogy: A census, then a lie-detector: the F2 counts the classes; the test cross names the genotype.
medium.examPointer: Name the F2 generation explicitly and call the second pairing a test cross.

modules.title: From Ratio to Probability
sourceHeadings: Predicting Probabilities of Outcomes from Monohybrid Crosses
modules.opening: The same grid converts directly into probabilities: with two heterozygous pea plants, three of the four cells carry the dominant phenotype, so any one offspring has a 75 percent chance of being tall and a 25 percent chance of being short.
keyPoints: Probabilities come from counting cells in the completed grid.
Tt crossed with Tt gives TT, two Tt and tt across four cells.
Three tall cells out of four means a 75 percent chance of tall.
The remaining cell means a 25 percent chance of short.

low.restatement: Count the tall boxes, divide by four, and that is your percentage.
low.analogy: A spinner with four equal sectors, three of them painted tall.
low.examPointer: Ratios describe the brood; percentages describe each single offspring.

medium.restatement: Each fertilisation is independent, so the percentage is a per-event chance, not a batch quota.
medium.analogy: Four coins tossed do not guarantee exactly three heads, though the chance per coin stays 75 percent in this analogy.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish ratio language from probability language in answers.

glossary.definition: A grid that pairs parental alleles to list every possible offspring genotype.
An inheritance pattern controlled by a single gene.
The first offspring generation from a cross between pure-breeding parents.
The generation produced by interbreeding the F1 offspring.
The count of phenotype classes among the offspring, such as 3:1.
